 2   Q:   Please state your name and business address.

 3   A:   My name is Melissa K. Hardesty. My business address is 1200 Main, Kansas City,

 5   Q:   Are you the same Melissa K. Hardesty who submitted direct testimony on February

 9   Q:   On whose behalf are you testifying?

10   A:   I am testifying on behalf of Evergy Metro, Inc. d/b/a Evergy Missouri Metro (“Evergy

11        Missouri Metro,” “EMM,” or the “Company”).

12   Q:   What is the purpose of your testimony?

13   A:   The purpose of my testimony is to respond to true-up direct testimony of Missouri Public

14        Service Commission Staff (“Staff”) witness Nathan Bailey regarding the property tax

15        tracker.

  1                                        II. PROPERTY TAX TRACKER

 2   Q:       What does Section 393.400 require with respect to property taxes?

 3   A:       Section 393.400 1 requires EMM to defer to a regulatory asset or liability account the

 4            difference between its “property tax expenses actually incurred” and the property taxes “on

 5            which the revenue requirement used to set rates in the corporation's most recently

 6            completed general rate proceeding was based.” The balance is included in rates through

 7            an amortization over a reasonable period in EMM’s subsequent general rate proceedings,

 8            and the rate base is adjusted to reflect the unamortized balance.

 9   Q:       What balance does Staff recommend for the property tax tracker for rate base

10            treatment?

11   A:       Mr. Bailey recommends a balance of $6,516,496 as of June 30, 2026, to be included for

12            rate base treatment. In comparison, the Company recommends a balance of $31,626,790,

13            which includes the $4,052,953 as deferred from August 28, 2022, to January 8, 2023.

14   Q:       Do the Company and Staff agree on prior property tax treatment for prior years?

15   A:       Yes and No. The Company and Staff disagree as it pertains to the stub period - August 28,

16            2022, the effective date of Section 393.400 through January 8, 2023, the day before EMM

17            rates became effective in Case No. ER-2022-0129. 2 Staff's position is that reaching back

18            to the 2018 rate case is not consistent with the legislation's language of “recently completed

19            general rate proceeding,” and that a discrete, agreed-upon base level of property taxes did

20            not exist in the 2018 rate case. 3 However, as discussed in Evergy witness Ron Klote’s

 7   Q:         Do the Company and Staff agree regarding property tax treatment in 2026?

 8   A:         No. The Company and Staff disagree on the appropriate treatment of 2026 property taxes.

 9              Because those taxes will not be paid in full until December 2026, the disagreement was not

10              apparent at the time of Staff’s direct filing, which relied on data through December 2025

11              and therefore did not reflect Staff’s proposed treatment for 2026. The issue first became

12              apparent in Staff’s true-up direct filing, when Staff updated its adjustment that applied a

13              2026 methodology that differs from approaches Staff has used in prior dockets.

  1   Q:         How has Staff calculated the 2026 portion of the tracker through the June 30, 2026,

2               true-up date?

3    A:         Staff improperly compares the property tax expense in base rates, prorated through June

 4              30, 2026, to the property taxes EMM paid through the same date. 6 The Company

 5              recognizes property tax expense on a generally consistent basis throughout the year.

 6              However, the Company pays most of its annual property taxes at the end of the year. Only

 7              approximately 24% of EMM’s annual property tax payments were made by June 30, 2026,

 8              with the remaining expense to be paid in December. ￼Staff prorates the annual property

 9              tax expense in base rates to the first half of 2026 but does not align property taxes incurred

10              on a comparable basis. Instead, Staff compares that prorated base-rate level to cash

11              payments that, for most of EMM’s 2026 property taxes, had not yet been disbursed by June

12              30, 2026, but rather only incurred. 7 As a result, Staff compares approximately one-half of

13              the annual property tax expense embedded in base rates to only approximately 24% of the

14              annual property tax payments expected for 2026, thereby understating property tax

15              deferrals through true-up date. The timing mismatch produces a credit to the tracker for

16              2026 of ($14,422,643) that offsets the $20,939,139 of deferrals that the tracker

17              accumulated from January 9, 2023, through December 31,2025.

18   Q:         Does Section 393.400 measure property taxes when they are paid?

19   A:         No. Section 393.400 refers to property tax expenses actually incurred, not paid. As I

20              explained in my direct testimony, the tracker defers the difference between the actual

21              property tax expense incurred and the property tax expense embedded in base rates from

22              EMM’s most recent general rate case, No. ER-2022-0129. An expense is incurred when


     6
         See N. Bailey Surrebuttal/True-Up Direct at 2, 22
     7
         Id. at 7.

                                                             4
  1        the obligation to pay it arises, not when the cash is disbursed. EMM property tax assessed

 2        values are set based on information available at January 1 each year and is it obligated to

 3        pay the taxes based on this value. The value is not set when the taxes are due to be paid.

 4        Therefore, under generally accepted accounting rules it incurs and accrues a pro-rata

 5        portion of its property tax expense throughout the year based on January 1 assessed values.

 6        Therefore, EMM has incurred property taxes through June 30, 2026, but has not paid such

 7        expense.

 8   Q:   What approach does the Company recommend for the 2026 portion of the tracker?

 9   A:   The Company would agree to use EMM’s 2025 actual property taxes as the estimate of its

10        2026 property taxes, with those amounts prorated through June 30, 2026, and compared to

11        the base-rate level for the same period. This approach puts both sides of the comparison

12        on the same basis and is also the same approach that Staff witness Karen Lyons used in the

13        2024 Evergy Missouri West rate case, No. ER-2024-0189.             Under the Company’s

14        approach, the 2026 portion of the tracker would be $4,568,778. This represents half the

15        amount of actual 2025 property taxes that exceeded the base level in the 2025 year.

16        Although the Company proposed using the best available estimate of $6,634,698 at June

17        2026 in its true-up adjustment in calculating the 2026 portion of the tracker, which also

18        reflected putting both sides of the comparison on the same basis, the Company would agree

19        to the approach described above of using the 2025 actual property taxes as the estimate for

20        the portion of 2026 through June 30, 2026, true-up.

  1   Q:         Does Staff rely on EMM’s last known annual property taxes elsewhere in its

 2              testimony?

 3   A:         Yes. Mr. Bailey testifies that the base level Staff has recommended for every regulated

 4              Missouri utility that has filed a general rate case since the property tax tracker legislation

 5              took effect was based on the last known annual amount of property taxes. 8 The Company’s

 6              approach to 2026 tracker deferrals uses the same measure, i.e., EMM’s last known annual

 7              property taxes which are its 2025 actual property taxes.

 8   Q:         Has Staff used prior-year actual property taxes to estimate a partial year in a prior

 9              case?

10   A:         Yes. Staff witness Kimberly Bolin testified in Case No. WR-2020-0344, a Missouri-

11              American Water Company proceeding, that the Commission has a long-standing practice

12              of using a historical test year approach because “customer rates are established using actual

13              past levels of revenues, expenses, and rate base. Test year revenues/expense/rate base

14              amounts are the starting point for rate analysis and are subject to both normalization

15              adjustments to eliminate abnormal test year amounts and annualization adjustment to

16              reflect the latest known trends in the utility’s cost structure.” 9

17                      In applying the historical test year, Staff has previously used the “known and

18              measurable standard.” Ms. Bolin testified in Case No. ER-2021-0312 that the “known and

19              measurable” standard requires that only the costs associated with events that have actually

20              occurred or are certain to occur, and for which the financial impact can be accurately

21              quantified, should be reflected in utility rates. If adhered to, the known and measurable

11   Q:       How do the Company's concerns with Staff's tracker balance affect the annual

12           amortization amount?

13   A:      The Company's concerns relate to the calculation of the unamortized tracker balance, as

14           discussed above, rather than Staff's proposed four-year amortization period. Because the

15           annual amortization amount is derived directly from the unamortized tracker balance,

16           correcting the issues identified by the Company increases the balance subject to

17           amortization and correspondingly increases the annual amortization amount. Under the

18           Company's approach, the annual amortization amount would be approximately $7,906,698

19           per year, compared to Staff's proposed annual amortization amount of $1,629,124.

  1                  III. NUCLEAR PRODUCTION TAX CREDIT TRACKER

 2   Q:   How did Staff’s nuclear production tax credit adjustment change from its direct filing

 3        to true-up?

 4   A:    In its direct filing, Staff’s adjustment had two cost of service components: an amortization

 5        of the 2025 nuclear PTCs and an assumed annual level of ongoing nuclear PTC benefits.

6         At true-up, Staff removed the amortization associated with the 2025 credits but retained

7         the assumed ongoing level. Although that change addressed one part of the adjustment, it

8         did not resolve the fundamental issue with including an estimated future benefit in current

9         rates.

10   Q:   Why is Staff’s remaining ongoing nuclear PTC adjustment incorrect?

11   A:   Staff continues to treat an estimated future tax benefit as though it has already been realized.

12        As of the June 30, 2026, true-up date, the Company had not completed a sale of nuclear

13        PTCs, and the amount ultimately available depends on unresolved tax guidance, the

14        method used to calculate the credits, actual nuclear generation, market conditions, and the

15        price and costs of any future transfer. Staff’s estimate therefore is not a known and

16        measurable amount appropriate for inclusion in base rates.

17   Q:   Would approving the nuclear PTC tracker protect customers without Staff’s ongoing

18        adjustment?

19   A:   Yes. The tracker records the net benefit when a nuclear PTC is actually used to reduce the

20        Company’s tax liability or monetized through a sale, including the actual proceeds and

21        directly related transaction costs. That approach ensures customers receive the benefit

22        actually realized while avoiding a rate reduction based on credits that may be calculated




                                                     8
 1        differently, sold at a discount, delayed, or not realized at all. Accordingly, the appropriate

2        amount of assumed ongoing nuclear PTC benefits in the revenue requirement is zero.

3   Q:   Does that conclude your true-up rebuttal testimony?

4   A:   Yes, it does.
